docs.title: LLM Engineering Course
docs.text:
Learn how language models work by building the important pieces yourself, then use those pieces to develop a model for a realistic company use case.

Start with setup and the learning guide. The guide names prerequisites and checkpoints; the glossary explains unfamiliar terms. No prior machine learning is required.

docs.title: Two entry paths
docs.text:
• Standalone path: includes Python, mathematics, neural-network, and PyTorch foundations.
  • Godot RL bridge: uses a diagnostic to skip concepts already demonstrated in the Godot RL course.

Both paths start with Unit 0, continue through the diagnostic and learning-path check, and converge before text tokenization. Every skipped foundation keeps a re-entry link.

The standalone foundations track is now executable: Python/NumPy, tensor shapes, probability and cross-entropy, a trainable neuron, MLP/backpropagation, a tiny autograd engine, and a PyTorch checkpoint. Godot-RL graduates can take the compact bridge and prove only the missing LLM-specific concepts. Both paths now continue into the executable bigram language-model baseline, the from-scratch byte-level BPE tokenizer, the versioned data pipeline and embedding path, and self-attention from first principles. Continue with the Mini-GPT decoder and its core gate, then reproducible training, data quality, evaluation and profiling.

Every required outcome has a CPU route. Run the hardware and cost preflight before choosing a larger profile.

docs.title: What you will build
docs.text:
• a bigram language-model baseline;
  • a BPE tokenizer;
  • self-attention and a decoder-only transformer;
  • a small GPT-style model with training and evaluation;
  • instruction and preference fine-tuning;
  • a synthetic-data pipeline with quality gates;
  • an optimized local inference service;
  • a reproducible company-model capstone.

Development status

Unit 0 now has an executable Tiny-LM vertical slice and is ready for its required five-learner pilot. The diagnostic, hardware gates, and neural- foundations track, reproducible bigram baseline, byte-level BPE lab, versioned data pipeline with embeddings, and self-attention lab are available. M2 adds the decoder, core gate and model card; M3 adds resumable CPU training, provenance audits, paired evaluation and measured profiling. Later company-model units and larger supplied datasets remain planned. The real five-learner pilot is still open; automated checks do not establish learner comprehension or issue a certificate.

docs.title: Choose an adaptation with evidence
docs.text: Prerequisites: company requirements, held-out evaluation and SFT/LoRA. Nordlicht Workspace is fictional. Its narrow support workflow needs routing, correct policy facts, valid JSON and safe escalation. Those are separate quality axes; one average cannot replace inspection of severe failures.

docs.title: Start with the cheapest adequate change
docs.text:
Method What changes? Appropriate first question Main cost or risk Prompting Instructions/context only Does clearer output guidance suffice? Context and inference cost Retrieval Relevant approved documents in context Are facts changing or must sources be cited? Retrieval quality and permissions DAPT/TAPT LM weights from domain/task text Is unfamiliar language the actual bottleneck? Forgetting; no explicit answer format Full SFT All selected model weights Do many representative answers justify full updates? Gradients/optimizer state and overfit LoRA Small A/B matrices on frozen weights Can a small update teach task behavior? Limited capacity; base remains in memory QLoRA LoRA plus a quantized frozen base Does a tested 4-bit backend fit the host? Kernel/backend constraints and quantization error

QLoRA retains a frozen 4-bit base and trains higher-precision adapters. NF4 uses a codebook designed for normally distributed weights; double quantization also compresses quantization scale constants. It does not train every base parameter in four bits. QLoRA's paper describes these mechanisms. The pinned bitsandbytes backend documentation lists CUDA, XPU, HPU and supported Linux/Windows CPU platforms, not this macOS MPS host. QLoRA is unavailable in this measured environment. No simulated 4-bit experiment is presented as QLoRA evidence.

docs.title: Compare like with like
docs.text:
A fair paired comparison fixes the base, tokenizer, train/dev splits, seed, sequence treatment, batch size, optimizer and steps. Record trainable parameters, wall time and the exact memory scope. Equal steps do not mean equal compute, and one shared learning rate is a controlled baseline rather than optimal tuning for every method. Never compare tiny random MiniGPT and pretrained SmolLM2 as though only the adapter method changed.

For the CPU MiniGPT pair, seed 7, 120 steps, batch 4 and AdamW LR 0.003 are fixed. Sixteen training and eight independently authored development cases are used. The tokenizer is trained only on training text. Generated corpora/weights stay in ignored artifacts/; executable recipes and compact numerical evidence are tracked.

MiniGPT method Trainable parameters Train NLL Dev NLL General-control NLL Dev correct Format failures Initial random base 40,416 6.163 6.181 6.337 0/8 8/8 Full SFT 40,416 0.488 3.816 7.309 0/8 5/8 Manual LoRA, rank 4 3,968 3.768 4.469 7.212 0/8 8/8

Full SFT's train/dev gap is 3.816 − 0.488 = 3.328 nats. Its general-control loss increases by 0.973; LoRA increases it by 0.875. These two simple completion controls show worsening likelihood, not a comprehensive general capability benchmark. The original random model had no established general competence to preserve. Lower train loss and fewer trainable parameters do not satisfy the company gate. Both adaptations are rejected for deployment; keep the base and investigate data coverage, prompt consistency and evaluation failures before another development run.

Measured runtime, memory and the separately identified real pretrained CPU/MPS experiment are recorded in docs/baselines/sft-lora-v1.md and docs/model-cards/company-adapter-v1.md. The PEFT example evaluates identical cases before training, after training, after adapter reload and after merge.

docs.title: Predict → Trace → Build → Break → Measure → Explain
docs.text:
1. Predict: Which method can update tomorrow's policy without weight training?
  2. Trace: Follow an approved document through prompt context versus training data.
  3. Build: Run the paired CPU recipe and inspect one failed generation per domain.
  4. Break: Raise learning rate or train on one repeated answer; predict collapse first.
  5. Measure: Compare train/dev gap, JSON failures, critical safety and general control.
  6. Explain: Choose rollback or promotion using the company acceptance criteria.

docs.title: Independent exercise
docs.text:
Candidate A has 7/8 correct cases but fails one critical secret request. Candidate B has 6/8 correct, no critical failures, and twice the inference latency. The contract requires zero critical failures and latency below 200 ms; B takes 240 ms. Decide whether either can be promoted, then propose the next measurement without touching gold.

Hint

Hard acceptance gates do not compensate for each other. Use development cases for iterative changes; gold remains reserved for the final sealed decision.

Reference answer

Neither passes: A violates safety, B violates latency. Preserve the current deployed version, inspect A's escalation behavior and profile B under the same hardware/load. Re-evaluate development after a concrete change. Do not claim a gold improvement from a lower training loss.

Checkpoint: explain when retrieval, continued pretraining and SFT solve different problems; read a fair paired scorecard; distinguish storage savings from peak memory; reject a promising adapter when a required gate fails.

docs.title: T04 — Self-attention as a number experiment
docs.text: ← T03 data pipeline · Course home

docs.title: Learning outcome
docs.text:
In 90–110 minutes, you will implement scaled dot-product attention from first principles, verify it against a hand calculation and against PyTorch's fused reference, prove that a causal mask blocks the future, extend one head to several, and diagnose four deliberately broken variants by measurement rather than by intuition.

The lab runs on the embedded batches from T03, so attention operates on real tokens rather than on random noise.

docs.title: Predict · What can a position know?
docs.text:
Before running anything, predict:

  1. what shape the score matrix has for a batch [B,T,D] with H heads;
  2. why the scores are divided by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) and what happens without it;
  3. whether attention weights in row t may be non-zero to the right of t.

Then run the CPU reference:

python examples/run_attention_lab.py

It prints the report and writes artifacts/attention/heatmap-head-0.svg (both stay out of Git).

docs.title: Trace · Compute one example by hand
docs.text:
hand_check_example() uses three tokens in two dimensions, with queries, keys, and values all equal to

\[ X=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}. \]

Attention is five explicit steps:

\[ S=\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}},\qquad S'=\mathrm{mask}(S),\qquad A=\mathrm{softmax}(S'),\qquad Y=AV \]

With \(d_k = 2\), row 1 compares scores \(0\) and \(1/\sqrt{2}\), so its weights are

\[ \left[\frac{1}{1+e^{1/\sqrt{2}}},\ \frac{e^{1/\sqrt{2}}}{1+e^{1/\sqrt{2}}}\right] = [0.330,\ 0.670]. \]

Row 0 may only read itself and therefore returns \(V_0=[1,0]\) unchanged. Compute row 2 yourself and compare it against the report before continuing. If your number differs, you have found either your error or the code's.

docs.title: Build · One head
docs.text:
SingleHeadSelfAttention holds three projections and nothing else. Trace the shapes for a batch [4,23,16] with head_dim=8:

Value Shape Meaning inputs [4,23,16] embedded tokens from T03 queries, keys, values [4,23,8] what each position asks, offers, and carries scores [4,23,23] similarity of every query to every key weights [4,23,23] row-normalized; each row sums to 1 output [4,23,8] value mixture per position

Two properties are asserted, not assumed: every row sums to one, and future_attention_mass(weights) is exactly 0.0. The second is the causal mask doing its job — a [T,T] boolean lower triangle that sets blocked scores to \(-\infty\) before the softmax, so they receive exactly zero weight rather than a small one.

Additional boolean masks restrict the causal mask by intersection: True means allowed, but cannot unlock a future key when causal=True. Masks must cover [T,T]; for per-example multi-head masks use [B,1,T,T]. Every query must retain at least one allowed key; fully blocked rows raise ValueError before softmax. To study unrestricted attention, explicitly set causal=False.

The JSON report represents masked scores as the string "-inf", because JSON has no infinity number. Computation still uses floating-point negative infinity. Heatmap labels follow the selected batch sequence (the CLI uses sequence 0).

docs.title: Build · Several heads
docs.text:
MultiHeadSelfAttention projects to the full width, splits it into H heads of D/H dimensions, attends per head, merges, and mixes the result once more:

Value Shape Meaning queries [4,4,23,4] [B,H,T,D/H] after split_heads weights [4,4,23,23] one attention matrix per head output [4,23,16] merged heads, projected back to model width

The reshape is the part that fails silently, because a wrong view/transpose order still produces the correct shape. head_by_head_reference therefore recomputes the same result with an explicit Python loop over heads and no reshape at all. The reference configuration reaches a maximum difference of 0.000; PyTorch's fused scaled_dot_product_attention differs by 2.4e-7, which is float32 arithmetic, not a bug.

gradient_check compares autograd's input gradients with central finite differences in float64 and reports a maximum relative error of 3.3e-11.

docs.title: Break · Four defects, four measurements
docs.text:
diagnose_broken_variants runs each defect on the same inputs and records what catches it:

Variant Symptom Caught by no_mask future attention mass 179.05 instead of 0.0 causality check no_scaling weight entropy 1.82 versus 2.11 — attention too peaked entropy comparison wrong_transpose [d_k,d_k] score matrix shape check softmax_over_queries row sums off by 3.82 normalization check

The transpose defect only raises when T != d_k. silent_transpose_case() sets both to 4: nothing raises, the shape matches, and only comparing values reveals a maximum difference of 1.007 and a future mass of 1.21. A test that checks shapes alone would pass on a model that reads the future.

For each variant, answer: which of your tests would have failed first?

docs.title: Measure · Read the heatmap
docs.text:
Open artifacts/attention/heatmap-head-0.svg. Rows are query positions, columns are keys; the upper right is empty because of the mask. Early positions must concentrate their weight on few keys — position 0 has exactly one choice — while later rows spread it out.

Change one factor and predict the effect first:

python examples/run_attention_lab.py --heads 1
python examples/run_attention_lab.py --heads 8

More heads at the same width mean a smaller head_dim, so each head compares in a narrower space. The parameter count stays at 1024 for embedding_dim=16 regardless of the head count — heads split capacity, they do not add it.

See the versioned attention reference for the reference values and the change protocol.

docs.title: Explain · Your attention paragraph
docs.text:
Write one paragraph that names:

  • the shape and meaning of queries, keys, values, scores, weights, and output;
  • why the scores are scaled by \(\sqrt{d_k}\);
  • how the mask enforces causality, and at which step it is applied;
  • what splitting into heads changes and what it does not;
  • the measurement that catches each of the four defects;
  • the two references your implementation was checked against.

docs.title: Completion gate
docs.text:
You pass when you can derive one row of the attention matrix by hand and your report proves the implementation. Required evidence:

  • your own row-2 calculation matching hand_check in the report;
  • [B,H,T,T] weights with row sums of 1 and future mass 0.0;
  • agreement with the head-by-head reference and with PyTorch (< 1e-5);
  • a gradient check below 1e-5 relative error;
  • all four broken variants with the measurement that catches each;
  • one heatmap, read out loud in two sentences.

Run the automated contract checks:

pytest tests/test_attention.py

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
One attention layer mixes information across positions but cannot transform it much. Next, you will add residual paths, normalization, and a feed-forward network to build a full decoder block and a Mini-GPT.

← T03 data pipeline · Course home

→ Mini-GPT decoder · Learning guide

docs.title: T01 — Bigram language-model baseline
docs.text: ← F06 checkpoint · Course home

docs.title: Learning outcome
docs.text: In 75–90 minutes, you will build and compare a count-based and a neural character bigram model. You will trace the complete next-token training loop, measure negative log-likelihood on isolated data, sample reproducibly, and use fixed evidence to decide whether training improved the baseline. The supplied CC0 corpus is generated locally; you need no data of your own.

docs.title: Predict · What can one character know?
docs.text:
A bigram model sees only the current character when predicting the next one. Before running the code, predict:

  1. which tensor shapes result from a batch [B,T];
  2. whether a learned table can beat uniform probability 1/33;
  3. why it still cannot remember the word before the current character.

Then run the CPU reference:

python examples/run_bigram_baseline.py --device cpu

Keep the JSON output. It records the configuration, split hashes, losses, fixed prompts, probabilities, and seeded samples for both models.

docs.title: Trace · Split before making windows
docs.text:
split_corpus shuffles 16 unique lines with seed 7 and creates 12 training, 2 validation, and 2 test lines. Only then does CharacterWindowDataset create overlapping next-character examples. This order prevents nearly identical windows from the same line leaking into multiple partitions.

For block_size=16 and batch_size=8, a batch has:

Value Shape Meaning inputs [8,16] current character IDs targets [8,16] the same windows shifted by one logits [8,16,33] one score per possible next character

The validation split chooses experiments. The test split is read only for the final report; repeatedly tuning on it would turn it into training information.

docs.title: Build · Count probabilities
docs.text:
The count model records how often target character y follows source character x. Additive smoothing gives every transition non-zero probability:

\[ P(y\mid x)=\frac{N(x,y)+\alpha}{\sum_z N(x,z)+\alpha V} \]

Here V=33 and alpha=0.25. Inspect fit_count_bigram: counts become probabilities, then log-probabilities become the fixed transition logits. There is no optimizer and no gradient descent in this model.

Use bigram_probabilities(model, "the ") and verify that all 33 values are finite, non-negative, and sum to one.

docs.title: Build · Learn the same table with gradients
docs.text:
TinyBigramLM contains one trainable [33,33] transition table. An input ID selects a row. Cross-entropy compares that row with the observed next ID.

For targets \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\), mean negative log-likelihood is

\[ \mathrm{NLL}=-\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \log P(y_i\mid x_i). \]

For a one-hot next-character target, this is exactly cross-entropy. Trace one iteration in train_neural_bigram in this order:

  1. load a seeded batch and move it to the selected device;
  2. clear old gradients;
  3. compute logits and cross-entropy;
  4. run backward and reject non-finite gradients;
  5. update parameters with AdamW;
  6. measure validation loss without gradients.

Explain what would go wrong if step 2 happened only once before the loop.

docs.title: Break · Expose weak evidence
docs.text:
Run an intentionally under-trained comparison:

python examples/run_bigram_baseline.py --device cpu --steps 1

One training batch is not evidence that an experiment generalizes. A falling batch loss alone is also insufficient. Keep the split, seed, and prompts fixed, then restore 60 steps:

python examples/run_bigram_baseline.py --device cpu --steps 60

Now change only the learning rate to 0.02. Predict the result, run it, and record whether the validation loss—not merely training loss—improved.

docs.title: Measure · Compare like with like
docs.text:
The reference configuration is seed 7, 60 steps, learning rate 0.2, block_size=16, and batch_size=8. On the course environment, the count model has validation loss about 1.861; the neural model moves from about 3.497 to 1.547 and therefore beats both its initial state and the count baseline. Minor floating-point differences are acceptable; the direction and evidence contract are not.

The prompts "the ", "a ", and "each " are fixed. Each report includes the three most likely next characters and a CPU-seeded sample. Generated text will remain locally plausible but incoherent because a bigram has one-character context. That limitation is a result, not a sampling bug.

See the versioned reference baseline for hashes, thresholds, and the reproduction command.

docs.title: Explain · Your model card paragraph
docs.text:
Write one paragraph that names:

  • the input, target, parameter, and logits shapes;
  • how counts and gradient descent estimate the same conditional distribution;
  • why cross-entropy is negative log-likelihood here;
  • which partition supports model selection and which supports final reporting;
  • the measured validation comparison;
  • the one-character context limitation.

docs.title: Completion gate
docs.text:
You pass when you can recreate the full data → tokens → batches → logits → probabilities → loss → gradients → update → validation → sampling loop without looking at the diagram, and your saved report proves whether one controlled change improved the fixed baseline. Required evidence:

  • disjoint split counts and SHA-256 hashes;
  • asserted [B,T] and [B,T,V] shapes;
  • finite normalized probabilities;
  • initial, final, validation, and test losses;
  • all three fixed prompts with the same seed;
  • a conclusion based on validation loss, including a result that did not help.

Run the automated contract checks:

pytest tests/test_bigram.py

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
The character vocabulary is fixed and cannot represent useful subwords. Continue with the byte-level BPE tokenizer and measure how vocabulary and sequence length change the same modelling problem.

← F06 checkpoint · → BPE tokenizer

docs.title: T02 — Byte-level BPE tokenizer from scratch
docs.text: ← T01 Bigram baseline · Course home

docs.title: Learning outcome
docs.text: In 90–120 minutes, you will train, encode, and decode with your own byte-level Byte Pair Encoding tokenizer. You will preserve arbitrary Unicode, make special tokens explicit, visualize merge decisions and token lengths, and compare the small course vocabulary with a production tokenizer. No learner-owned data, cloud, or accelerator is required.

docs.title: Predict · Characters are not bytes
docs.text:
Predict the UTF-8 byte counts of A, ü, 你, and 👩🏽‍💻. Then check:

for text in ("A", "ü", "你", "👩🏽‍💻"):
    print(text, list(text.encode("utf-8")))

A Python string contains Unicode text; storage and models need integers. UTF-8 maps every valid string to bytes 0..255. BPE starts from those 256 byte IDs and learns larger pieces. Therefore ordinary text never needs an unknown token, even when its language or emoji never appeared in training.

Run the complete reference:

python examples/run_tokenizer_lab.py

It writes only ignored local evidence under artifacts/tokenizer/:

  • report.json — corpus hash, vocabulary, merge trace, token pieces and lengths;
  • merge-trace.svg — the first ordered merge decisions;
  • token-lengths.svg — UTF-8 bytes versus course and production token counts.

docs.title: Trace · One merge with concrete numbers
docs.text:
For abababab, UTF-8 starts as eight IDs:

97 98 97 98 97 98 97 98

The pair (97,98) occurs four times. Merge it into new ID 256:

256 256 256 256

Now adjacent pair (256,256) has frequency three; left-to-right replacement is non-overlapping and produces two ID 257 tokens. Pair counting and replacement are deliberately separate operations.

In the real run, train_byte_bpe repeats this loop:

  1. count every adjacent pair in the current training sequence;
  2. choose the highest frequency, breaking ties by the smaller ID pair;
  3. assign the next ID and replace non-overlapping occurrences;
  4. stop at the vocabulary budget or minimum frequency.

The deterministic tie-break, fixed corpus generator, and SHA-256 hash make the merge order reproducible.

docs.title: Build · Encode and decode
docs.text:
The reference vocabulary has 300 IDs:

Range Purpose 0..255 complete byte fallback 256..295 40 learned merge tokens 296..299 <|pad|>, <|bos|>, <|eos|>, <|unk|>

Encoding first converts ordinary text to UTF-8 bytes. It repeatedly applies the currently available merge with the earliest training rank. Decoding expands merge IDs back to bytes and performs one strict UTF-8 decode. Test the invariant:

text = "Grüezi 你好 👩🏽‍💻 cafe\u0301"
ids = tokenizer.encode(text)
assert tokenizer.decode(ids) == text

The composed é and decomposed e plus combining accent have different byte sequences. The tokenizer does not silently normalize either one; both roundtrip.

docs.title: Build · Treat control tokens deliberately
docs.text:
Registered special tokens become atomic only when explicitly allowed:

ids = tokenizer.encode(
    "<|bos|>hello<|eos|>",
    allowed_special={"<|bos|>", "<|eos|>"},
)

Without allowed_special, the same visible text is ordinary UTF-8 content. This distinction prevents an untrusted document from silently becoming a model control sequence. <|unk|> is reserved for interoperability; byte fallback means ordinary Unicode input never emits it.

docs.title: Break · Find the trade-off
docs.text:
Keep the corpus and minimum frequency fixed, then run:

python examples/run_tokenizer_lab.py --vocabulary-size 280
python examples/run_tokenizer_lab.py --vocabulary-size 340

Predict the direction first. A larger vocabulary usually shortens familiar training-like sequences, but enlarges the model's embedding and output matrices. For hidden size C, adding 60 tokens adds 60 × C embedding parameters and, without tied weights, another 60 × C output parameters.

Now encode a script absent from training. Token count may approach its UTF-8 byte count, yet decoding still succeeds. This separates efficiency from OOV: unfamiliar text can be inefficient without being unrepresentable.

docs.title: Measure · Compare with a production tokenizer
docs.text:
The lab imports tiktoken only after your implementation is trained and uses cl100k_base as a production reference. The library is not used to implement or validate the course BPE algorithm.

With vocabulary 300, the reference run produces:

Evaluation text UTF-8 bytes Course BPE cl100k_base English sentence 37 19 8 German/Latin accents 29 25 11 CJK and emoji 29 25 14 composed/decomposed accents 37 29 11 Total 132 98 44

The production tokenizer wins on length because it has a much larger vocabulary trained on vastly more varied data. The small course tokenizer remains useful: every merge is inspectable, its entire training procedure fits in one module, and all inputs still roundtrip.

See the versioned BPE baseline for the exact hash and acceptance contract.

docs.title: Explain · Make the engineering decision
docs.text:
In your lab notes, answer:

  1. Why does byte fallback remove ordinary-text OOV failures?
  2. Why can an OOV-free tokenizer still produce long sequences?
  3. Which parameter matrices grow with the vocabulary?
  4. Why are merge rank and deterministic tie-breaking part of the model contract?
  5. Why must control tokens be distinguished from identical text in documents?
  6. Which vocabulary size would you choose for this corpus, and what evidence supports it?

docs.title: Completion gate
docs.text:
You pass when all Roundtrip and edge-case tests succeed and you can discuss the three-way trade-off among vocabulary size, sequence length, and OOV behavior. Submit:

  • your report.json with the expected training hash;
  • both SVG visualizations;
  • one Unicode and one special-token Roundtrip;
  • a 280-versus-300-or-340 controlled comparison;
  • a short decision that mentions sequence cost and embedding/output size.

Run the contract checks:

pytest tests/test_tokenizer.py

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
Next, the tokenizer enters a streaming data pipeline with manifests, contamination checks, deterministic shuffling, padding masks, and token batches for training.

← T01 Bigram baseline · Course home

docs.title: Capstone — From requirement to a reversible company model
docs.text:
Use only the committed code, manifests and baseline reports. Do not add real customer data or tune on the sealed gold cases.

  1. Write five must/can requirements for Nordlicht support.
  2. Rebuild the approved snapshot and prove its hash and contamination report.
  3. Score both transparent baselines on development cases.
  4. Compare prompting/retrieval, DAPT, full SFT/LoRA and DPO using the measured reports; record trainable parameters, latency/memory scope and failure cases.
  5. Select a candidate only after hard safety, provenance and local-processing gates pass.
  6. Run the sealed review with a human, then record the decision and corrections.
  7. Specify monitoring, a rollback checkpoint and an owner for each alert.

Your submission is a short decision record linking every claim to a command, hash, report or review row. Include two rejected alternatives and the evidence that would change the decision. The model may suggest a route; application code enforces authorization, secrets handling and export permissions.

Exit criteria: another learner can run the CPU recipes from a clean checkout, explain every metric, reproduce the baseline hashes and identify the exact step that rolls back a rejected adapter.

docs.title: M4 — Auditable company data
docs.text: Prerequisites: C01 strategy and data quality. Nordlicht Workspace is fictional, so every learner can inspect the complete source inventory without handling customer data.

docs.title: Build a snapshot before generating examples
docs.text:
source_inventory() contains current handbook facts plus deliberately planted fixtures: one deleted price, one restricted secret marker and one PII marker. build_snapshot() excludes those rows, records the reason, redacts email-like text and returns a stable SHA-256 hash. The hash identifies the exact approved snapshot used by later runs.

from llm_course.company_data import build_snapshot

snapshot = build_snapshot()
print(len(snapshot["documents"]), snapshot["sha256"])
print([row for row in snapshot["audit"] if row["decision"] != "include"])

The generator is deterministic and provenance-aware. Every instruction has a task (billing, access, export or escalate), a split, and source IDs. The filter rejects unknown actions, duplicate prompts, protected prompts, secrets, PII and unknown source IDs. instruction_records("train") returns 16 rows; instruction_records("development") returns 8. Neither imports protected gold.

Preference records reuse training prompts and pair an approved answer with a clearly unsafe alternative. The rejected answer is a teaching signal, never a production answer. Keep raw/generated data in ignored artifacts/; commit only the manifest and the reproducible code.

docs.title: Trace one record
docs.text:
1. Read the source ID and its license/access decision.
  2. Check that the response action matches the task and has exactly two string fields.
  3. Run contamination checks before training.
  4. Hash the final records and record the code/model revision.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Pass a candidate containing [SECRET_001], then a duplicate prompt, to filter_instruction_candidates. Predict both audit decisions before printing the result. Why must a deleted source be excluded even when its wording looks useful?

Reference answer

The secret row is excluded by the secret-marker filter and the repeated prompt is excluded by the duplicate filter. Deleted material is no longer an approved source, so retaining it would break provenance and policy review.

Checkpoint: explain the difference between a source snapshot, a training record, a development case and a protected gold case. Continue with company evaluation.

docs.title: M4 — Protected evaluation
docs.text:
The evaluator is authored separately from the training generator. It contains eight development cases for iteration and eight sealed gold cases for a final human review. gold_seal() checks the expected-response hash; it does not make human approval automatic.

score_predictions() reports exact accuracy, JSON format, route accuracy, per-task/per-severity results and critical safety failures. A critical request passes only when it routes to escalate and the answer contains no secret or PII disclosure. Average accuracy cannot hide a critical failure.

from llm_course.company_eval import (
    baseline_predictions, development_cases, score_predictions,
)

cases = development_cases()
report = score_predictions(cases, baseline_predictions(cases, "keyword_router"))
print(report["accuracy"], report["critical_failure_count"])

The review artifact docs/reviews/company-gold-v1.md prints every exact expected JSON string, the source/sample hashes and a human decision record. Do not tune on gold, copy it into training, or change a gold answer without recomputing the seal and rerunning baselines.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Compare always_escalate with keyword_router. Which metric can improve while the system still fails the contract? Add one invalid action and one secret-bearing answer to a critical case and inspect the case-level result.

Reference answer

Exact accuracy and route accuracy may look acceptable while format or safety fails. The evaluator rejects unknown actions and counts each critical safety failure separately; promotion requires zero critical failures.

Checkpoint: show a contamination report with no overlaps and explain why a held out development score is evidence for iteration, not proof of gold performance.

docs.title: C01 — Turn a company problem into a model decision
docs.text:
← Evaluation · Company data →

You can train a model now. This unit asks whether training is the right next action. Prerequisites: compare an unchanged baseline with a candidate, distinguish training from evaluation data, and explain why a lower NLL is a limited result. Allow two sessions: one to define the problem, one to interpret measured evidence.

docs.title: 1. Start with a workflow
docs.text:
Nordlicht Workspace is a fictional support-software company. A support agent receives a request about billing, account access or exports. The proposed system returns a small structured routing response; requests for secrets or unauthorized data must be escalated. It does not execute account changes. Invented facts and synthetic identifiers prevent the exercise from requiring real customer data.

Write requirements before selecting a model:

Requirement What to measure or inspect Users: support agents Can they inspect and correct the suggested route? Languages: English and German Report results separately by language. Must: correct route and valid JSON Score task and format independently. Must: escalate restricted requests Measure critical failures separately from average accuracy. Must: local processing Exclude a remote-only candidate before scoring quality. Must: known model/data provenance Inspect version, source permissions and license record. Budget: memory and response time Measure the same input length and device; disclose scope. Can: conversational explanation Add only after required behavior works.

The example is an advisory workflow with human review, not an autonomous access control mechanism. Authentication and authorization belong in application code.

docs.title: 2. Match the intervention to the gap
docs.text:
Observed gap First intervention Why Frequently changing facts Retrieval and tools Fetch the approved version at request time. Domain language is poorly predicted Test continued pretraining Learn its distribution, then check general-language regression. Correct format or response workflow is missing SFT, possibly with LoRA Provide target responses and supervise their tokens. Several responses work but one is preferred DPO Learn a relative preference from chosen/rejected pairs. Baseline already meets requirements No training Keep the simpler accepted system.

SFT specifies the objective and data. LoRA specifies which parameters can change; they are not competing tasks. QLoRA adds a frozen quantized base to low-rank adaptation. Training from scratch would need a reason such as an architecture experiment, not merely access to company documents.

For the routing workflow, compare a transparent rule baseline and a model under the same evaluator. If the rule baseline meets the narrow task, keep it as a serious option. An open model may justify its maintenance cost only when the required capability exceeds that narrow rule coverage.

docs.title: 3. Apply hard constraints before ranking
docs.text:
Suppose an online candidate scores 95% accuracy and a local one 80%. Local processing is mandatory. Averaging privacy and accuracy into a single score can wrongly recommend the online candidate. Instead:

  1. Eliminate candidates that fail any must requirement.
  2. Rank the remaining measured candidates by task quality, latency and memory.
  3. Preserve failed cases and uncertainty, not only the ranking.

Requirements and score_candidates implement these visible steps in src/llm_course/company_strategy.py. The default quality gate of 0.7 is an exercise threshold, not a production standard. A measured memory value must declare whether it means parameter bytes, tensor allocations or process peak.

from llm_course.company_strategy import Requirements, choose_strategy

requirements = Requirements(need="domain_language")
print(choose_strategy(requirements))  # No evidence: collect a baseline.
print(choose_strategy(requirements, domain_nll_gain=0.5,
                      general_nll_regression=0.1))

The second decision only starts a review of continued pretraining. It does not establish that instruction-following or support quality improved.

docs.title: 4. Count the work around training
docs.text:
TCO, total cost of ownership, includes preparation and recurring work. Use hypothetical currency units to practice the arithmetic:

  • Setup: 2 hours × 40 units/hour = 80.
  • Training: 1 compute-hour × 3 units/hour = 3.
  • Six months: each month 1 maintenance-hour × 40 plus 2 compute-hours × 3 = 46.
  • Total: 80 + 3 + 6*46 = 359 units.

These are invented rates, not vendor prices. Replace them with your own approved estimates, including data review, regression evaluation, deployment and rollback maintenance. Faster training can still be the more expensive system to maintain.

docs.title: 5. Predict → trace → build → break → measure → explain
docs.text:
Predict which approach the requirement selects. Trace one requirement to its measurement, then build a scorecard for the shared company task. Break it by giving the best-quality candidate an incompatible processing location. Measure the remaining candidates on identical cases. Explain at least two rejected alternatives, including what new evidence would change the decision.

Exercise: a company needs fresh export limits and strict JSON. Propose a system with separate responsibilities. Which part needs current facts? Which part could benefit from SFT? Do not put access rights into model weights.

Hint A single user-facing response can combine retrieved facts, deterministic schema validation and a trained formatter. Select a mechanism for each observed gap. Reference answer Retrieve approved current limits, enforce access in the application, and validate the output schema. Try prompting or a deterministic formatter first. Use SFT/LoRA only if the unchanged evaluation shows a remaining response-format gap. Reject continued pretraining for freshness and DPO for adding missing facts.

Checkpoint: another learner can trace every chosen component to a requirement, a measured baseline gap and a reproducible acceptance test. Continue with company data, then protected evaluation.

docs.title: M4 — Continued pretraining without losing the baseline
docs.text:
Continued pretraining (also called domain-adaptive pretraining, DAPT) continues the language-model objective on approved domain text. It teaches vocabulary and style distributions; it does not directly teach a JSON response contract.

run_continued_pretraining.py uses the approved company snapshot, byte-level fallback tokenization, disjoint domain held-outs and two general controls. It trains a tiny CPU model, saves an immutable base, resumes from an interrupted checkpoint, and can roll back by reloading the base.

.venv/bin/python examples/run_continued_pretraining.py --seeds 7 19 43

The measured seeds improved domain NLL by 0.359–0.411 nats while general-control NLL regressed by 0.032–0.109 nats. The report therefore keeps the candidate for further review rather than promoting it. Exact resume and rollback identity are strong engineering checks; they are not a quality claim.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Why are a domain gain and a general regression reported separately? Which change would make this experiment invalid: adding a general held-out sentence to the training text, or changing only the learning-rate seed?

Reference answer

Separate scores expose forgetting. Adding held-out text contaminates the test; a preregistered seed change is a new run that must be recorded, not hidden.

Checkpoint: state a promotion threshold, name the rollback artifact and explain why DAPT must be followed by instruction evaluation.

docs.title: T03 — Data pipeline & embeddings
docs.text: ← T02 byte-level BPE · Course home

docs.title: Learning outcome
docs.text:
In 75–90 minutes, you will build a versioned mini data pipeline that turns raw text into embedded batches, and you will be able to name the shape and meaning of every tensor on the way. You will split documents before creating windows, pack a token stream, pad variable-length sequences, mask padding out of the loss, seed the DataLoader, and measure leakage instead of hoping it is absent.

The pipeline runs on two encoders: the Unit-0 character vocabulary plus three special tokens, or the byte-level BPE tokenizer from T02. Only the DocumentEncoder object changes; every later stage keeps working, which is what makes the boundary between tokenization and pipeline visible.

docs.title: Predict · Where does a batch come from?
docs.text:
Before running anything, predict:

  1. how many [4,12] batches 470 training tokens produce;
  2. which positions of a padded batch must not reach the loss;
  3. whether splitting fixed-length windows randomly is as safe as splitting documents randomly.

Then run the CPU reference:

python examples/run_data_pipeline.py

Keep the JSON output. It records the version, configuration, split hashes, window counts, batch shapes, fill rates, batch hashes, embedding trace, and leakage numbers.

docs.title: Trace · Raw text to token IDs
docs.text:
normalize_documents strips whitespace, drops empty lines, and keeps the first copy of each exact duplicate. Deduplication happens before splitting: a document present twice would otherwise land in two partitions and turn memorization into apparent generalization.

encode_document then frames each document with the encoder's boundary tokens:

Token Character ID BPE ID Meaning content 0–32 0–295 bytes, merged pieces, or characters pad 33 296 filler; never contributes to the loss bos 34 297 document start eos 35 298 document end

decode_tokens prints special tokens by name, so <bos>a token<eos> is readable evidence rather than a mystery integer.

build_encoder trains BPE on the training documents only. A tokenizer trained on the whole corpus would carry validation and test statistics into every later measurement — leakage that no split can repair afterwards.

docs.title: Build · Two ways to reach a fixed shape
docs.text:
A model needs rectangular batches, but documents have different lengths. The pipeline implements both standard answers and measures them.

Packing. build_token_stream concatenates the encoded training documents into one stream of 470 tokens. SequenceWindowDataset cuts it into windows of block_size + 1 tokens and shifts them by one:

Value Shape Meaning input_ids [4,12] current token IDs labels [4,12] the same window shifted by one attention_mask [4,12] all ones; every position is real

With stride=12 the windows do not overlap and 1 tail token is dropped. With --stride 6 you get roughly twice as many windows over the same tokens, at the price of correlated examples.

Padding. PaddedDocumentDataset keeps one document per sample, and collate_batch right-pads a batch to its longest sequence:

Value Shape Meaning input_ids [4,39] tokens, <pad> after the document ends labels [4,39] targets, -100 after the document ends attention_mask [4,39] 1 for real tokens, 0 for padding

-100 is PyTorch's default ignore_index: cross-entropy skips those positions entirely. Padding that reaches the loss teaches the model to predict <pad>.

make_batch_loader wraps either dataset in a single-worker DataLoader with an explicit torch.Generator seed, so the batch order is part of the contract.

docs.title: Build · Token and position embeddings
docs.text:
TokenPositionEmbedding holds two tables:

  • token_embedding: [36,16] — one vector per token identity;
  • position_embedding: [64,16] — one vector per position index.

The forward pass adds them and zeroes padded positions:

\[ h_{b,t} = E_{\text{token}}[x_{b,t}] + E_{\text{pos}}[t] \]

The token table alone is position-blind: the same ID gets the same vector at position 0 and position 30. The sum is what lets a later attention layer tell the model from model the. Reference sizes: [4,39] IDs become [4,39,16] embeddings from 1600 parameters, and embedding.trace(batch) prints the whole chain with meanings.

docs.title: Break · Split after windowing
docs.text:
Run the deliberately wrong order, recorded in the same report under leakage.window_split_demo: build all 601 sliding windows first, then split them randomly. The result is 63 of 151 held-out windows appearing verbatim in training, and 149 of 151 overlapping training text by one or two positions.

Evaluation on that split measures copying, not learning. Compare it with the document split under leakage.document_split: 0 shared documents, and a measured window overlap of 0.300 (validation) and 0.216 (test), which stays inside the 0.5 budget.

Then force a failure to see the gate work:

python examples/run_data_pipeline.py --max-window-overlap 0.0

assert_no_leakage raises LeakageError. Overlap on template-generated text is expected and reported; unlimited overlap is not tolerated.

docs.title: Measure · Which shape wins
docs.text:
Loader Batch shape Real positions Fill rate packed [4,12] 468 / 468 1.000 padded [4,39] 458 / 480 0.954

Packing wastes nothing but crosses document boundaries, so a window may predict the start of one document from the end of another; <eos> is the signal that makes this learnable. Padding respects boundaries but pays for the longest sequence in every batch — the cost grows with length variance, not with the number of documents.

Now change only the encoder:

python examples/run_data_pipeline.py --encoder bpe
Measurement character byte-level BPE training tokens 470 223 packed windows 39 18 padded batch shape [4,39] [4,19] padded fill rate 0.954 0.894 embedding parameters 1600 5824 window overlap (validation) 0.300 0.000

Subwords halve the sequence length for the same text, so a fixed block_size covers roughly twice as much content — the reason context length is discussed in tokens, not characters. The vocabulary grows from 36 to 300, so the token table grows with it. The document split hashes stay identical, because the split happens on text and does not depend on the encoder.

Determinism is measurable too: batch_stream_fingerprint hashes every batch of a full pass. Two runs of the same version, config, and seed must return the same hashes. See the versioned data pipeline reference for the reference values and the change protocol.

docs.title: Explain · Your pipeline paragraph
docs.text:
Write one paragraph that names:

  • each stage from raw text to embeddings, with tensor shapes;
  • why deduplication and splitting happen before windowing;
  • what attention_mask and -100 each protect;
  • the trade-off between packing and padding, in fill rate;
  • what changes and what stays identical when you switch the encoder;
  • which numbers prove your batches are deterministic;
  • what your leakage budget is and why it is not zero here.

docs.title: Completion gate
docs.text:
You pass when you can redraw the chain text → documents → split → tokens → windows/padding → batch → embeddings without looking, and your saved report proves it. Required evidence:

  • split document counts and SHA-256 hashes;
  • [B,T] inputs, labels, and mask plus [B,T,D] embeddings;
  • padded positions holding <pad> in inputs and -100 in labels;
  • identical batch hashes across two runs with the same seed;
  • packed fill rate of 1.0 against the measured padded fill rate;
  • one character run and one BPE run of the same corpus;
  • 0 shared documents and a reported window overlap inside the budget.

Run the automated contract checks:

pytest tests/test_data_pipeline.py

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
The batches now carry meaning per position but no way to compare positions with each other. Next, you will build self-attention as a visible number experiment and give these embeddings context.

← T02 byte-level BPE · Course home

docs.title: Course data policy
docs.text:
Course home

The complete course must be possible without learners providing their own data.

docs.title: Planned supplied profiles
docs.text:
Profile Approximate size Purpose Starter 5–20 MB CPU exercises and smoke tests Local 100–500 MB normal local training path Extended 1–5 GB optional scaling exercises

The sizes above belong to M1A and are not yet supplied. Current offline fixtures are the 596-byte Unit-0 corpus, the multilingual BPE generator and the synthetic data-quality inventory. M2/M3 use these tiny course examples; no download or learner-owned dataset is required for their training path. The optional productive BPE comparison downloads its public tiktoken table on first use.

docs.title: Required metadata
docs.text: Every released data package must include a data card, schema, origin or generation method, license and source manifest, stable splits, hashes, version, generator seed, and quality reports.

docs.title: Gold evaluation separation
docs.text: The independent gold test set must not be included in model training, synthetic-data prompts, few-shot examples, or hyperparameter selection.

docs.title: Repository boundary
docs.text:
Only manifests, schemas, generators, and tiny offline fixtures belong in Git. Downloaded datasets, generated corpora, model weights, and training artifacts stay outside version control.

Unit 0 follows this rule with a committed manifest and deterministic generator. Its 596-byte CC0 corpus and derived prepared checkpoint are materialized under the ignored artifacts/unit0/ directory and verified by SHA-256.

The data-quality lab audits provenance, duplicates, synthetic sensitive/toxic markers and split contamination, then measures a misleading score caused by leakage. Manifests live under datasets/; corresponding data cards live under docs/data-cards/. Tests regenerate content and verify hashes.

docs.title: E02 — Data quality and provenance
docs.text: Course home · ← Training · → Evaluation

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Complete T03: distinguish a document, a token window and a split. Review loss if an apparently lower score still feels automatically better. Allow 60–90 minutes; this lab needs only CPU and generates fictional examples in memory.

You will explain where a training example came from, find contamination, repair training data without modifying the benchmark, and measure a false improvement. Provenance is the record of origin and processing. Governance means who may use a source, for what purpose, and under which retention/access rules.

docs.title: Predict: can perfect accuracy be meaningless?
docs.text:
Suppose training contains eight pairs of arbitrary card IDs and labels. Evaluation contains four different IDs. A program that only memorizes training answers gets 0/4 right. Copy the four evaluation pairs into training: it now gets 4/4 right. The algorithm did not improve; its input included the answers. This is leakage.

python examples/run_data_quality.py

The report is also saved to artifacts/data-quality/report.json. Expect:

Field Before After repair document count 9 4 exact duplicate pairs 2 0 near duplicate pairs 2 0 cross-split exact duplicate pairs 1 0 sensitive marker records 1 0 missing provenance records 1 0

In leakage_experiment, clean accuracy is 0, contaminated accuracy 1, and repaired accuracy 0. These are fractions, so 1 means 100%. The runner evaluates a literal lookup memorizer on arbitrary labels; it is a deliberately simple counterexample, not a language-model benchmark. Lower held-out LM loss needs the same protection.

docs.title: Trace: origin → audit → decision → version
docs.text:
Each QualityDocument holds id, text, split, source and license. The first two duplicated records have different IDs but identical text: checking IDs alone cannot find them. Normalizing case/whitespace helps detect superficial changes. Near matching compares sets of five-character pieces (shingles): if two sets share 8 pieces and their union contains 10, Jaccard similarity is 8/10 = 0.8. Our teaching threshold is 0.8. Similarity can also flag legitimate repeated wording, so inspect the evidence before applying this policy to real data.

from llm_course.data_quality import (
    generate_quality_documents, audit_documents, repair_documents,
)

raw = generate_quality_documents()
before = audit_documents(raw)
clean, decisions = repair_documents(raw)
assert before["cross_split_duplicates"] == [["leaked", "test"]]
assert audit_documents(clean)["ready"]
for decision in decisions:
    print(decision["id"], decision["action"], decision["reason"])

Repair retains the held-out copy and removes its training duplicate. It never silently edits validation/test. A defect inside held-out data raises an error: an independent review and a new benchmark version are needed. Sensitive markers such as [EMAIL_001] and [SECRET_001] become [REDACTED]; a [TOXIC] record is quarantined. These rules illustrate mechanisms. They do not detect all personal information, secret formats, toxicity or permission violations.

docs.title: Build: choose and explain a sampling mixture
docs.text:
A sampling weight controls how often a source is drawn. For 20 examples at 75% original / 25% synthetic, draw 15 and 5. Sampling with replacement can repeat rows; repeated draws are not additional unique knowledge.

from llm_course.data_quality import QualityDocument, deterministic_mixture

original = [doc for doc in clean if doc.split == "train"]
synthetic = [QualityDocument("new", "new authored teaching example", "train")]
mix = deterministic_mixture(
    {"original": original, "synthetic": synthetic},
    {"original": 0.75, "synthetic": 0.25}, size=20, seed=7,
)
assert sum(doc.id == "new" for doc in mix) == 5

Try 50/50 with the same size and seed. Before running, predict the new count. Report unique document count separately from sampled example count. Select weights on validation evidence, not on the protected final test.

docs.title: Break, measure and repair yourself
docs.text:
Create a copy of a validation row with a new ID and split="train". Predict why that is still leakage. Run the audit, remove the training copy, and show that held-out text and membership did not change. Then change the last character: can the near-duplicate rule still catch it? Record the score and any false positives.

Hint

Use dataclasses.replace(doc, id="copied", split="train"). The split must happen before making windows. Compare content, not only IDs.

Reference reasoning

A new ID does not make the text new. Exact matching detects the copied row; shingles can detect a small edit. Remove the train copy and preserve the original benchmark. The demonstration returns from 100% to 0% accuracy, honestly exposing the memorizer's lack of generalization.

docs.title: Source and license inventory
docs.text:
Before a real acquisition, record owner, source URL/version, license/permission, intended purpose, language, access group, personal-data categories, retention and delete/rebuild procedure. Public visibility is not permission to train. Unknown rights stay out of the training snapshot until reviewed. Automated redaction helps minimize exposure; it does not grant authorization or prove anonymization.

The course ships generators and manifests for Unit 0, BPE and this lab. All three have data cards under docs/data-cards/; each manifest records generator, license, UTF-8 byte count, SHA-256 and split policy. A hash identifies exact bytes: one changed space changes the identity. Never update a hash to make an unexplained mismatch disappear. A new version needs a new baseline and documented migration. The data policy distinguishes current tiny fixtures from planned larger supplied data packs. Do not commit generated corpora, real personal data or weights.

docs.title: Completion gate
docs.text: Run pytest tests/test_data_quality.py. Submit the before/after report, one repaired contamination defect, an explained mixture and a data card for an invented source. Explain why ready=true means only that these teaching checks passed, and why preserving test integrity can make a reported score worse.

docs.title: Diagnostic and learning path
docs.text: ← Unit 0 · Course home

docs.title: Learning outcome
docs.text:
In 45–60 minutes, you will collect evidence about the foundations you already control and receive a conservative route through the course. This is routing, not an exam: choosing more foundation work is always allowed and every shortcut is reversible.

Complete Unit 0 first. Every path joins again before text and tokenization.

docs.title: Two entry paths
docs.text:
Path Start here when What the diagnostic changes Standalone Little or no Python, mathematics, ML, or PyTorch experience Marks foundation blocks Required and still recognizes isolated strengths Godot-RL bridge You completed all or part of the Godot RL course Verifies transferable skills and removes repetition only where evidence is strong

Course completion and self-report never unlock a skip on their own.

docs.title: 1 · Experience inventory
docs.text:
Mark each item new, practised, or can explain and implement:

  • Python functions and tests;
  • tensor shapes;
  • logits, softmax, logarithms, and cross-entropy;
  • derivatives and the chain rule;
  • parameters, activations, loss, and backpropagation;
  • a PyTorch forward/backward/update cycle;
  • seeds, splits, and baselines;
  • observation, action, policy, reward, and trajectory.

Do not score this inventory. It helps distinguish environment trouble from a missing concept.

docs.title: 2 · Short theory check
docs.text:
Answer without searching first, then verify the reasoning.

  1. What does a list comprehension produce, and when is a generator safer?
  2. Why should a test check behaviour rather than a private implementation detail?
  3. X has shape [4, 8, 32] and W has shape [32, 64]. What is the shape of XW?
  4. In [B, T, C], which axis normally indexes token position?
  5. What probabilities does softmax assign to [0, 0], and what happens after adding the same constant to both logits?
  6. Why does a confident wrong prediction have a large cross-entropy loss?
  7. For L = (wx - y)², what is the derivative of L with respect to w?
  8. Why does an early layer's gradient depend on later operations?
  9. What is the difference between a parameter and an activation?
  10. What information from the forward pass is needed for backpropagation?
  11. Why are gradients normally cleared before the next optimizer step?
  12. Name an operation that can differ between training and evaluation.

Optional bridge prompt: map observation, action, policy, trajectory, and reward to LLM concepts, then name one place where the analogy fails.

docs.title: 3 · Coding check
docs.text: Documentation is allowed for a Review result; record when you used it.

docs.title: Task A — Python sequences
docs.text:
Write a function that turns the following sequence into adjacent input/target pairs:

["a", "b", "c", "d"]
[("a", "b"), ("b", "c"), ("c", "d")]

Add tests for an empty sequence, one item, and the normal case. Explain the time complexity.

docs.title: Task B — stable probabilities and shapes
docs.text:
With NumPy or PyTorch:

  • demonstrate a numerically stable softmax;
  • show that adding one constant to all logits leaves probabilities unchanged;
  • calculate cross-entropy for one correct target;
  • add shape and finite-value assertions.

docs.title: Task C — one PyTorch update
docs.text: Create a small Linear(3, 2) classifier and a batch shaped [4, 3]. Run a full training step: forward pass, cross-entropy against four class indices, gradient clearing, backward pass, finite-gradient check, and optimizer step. State the logit shape and explain what happens if gradients are never cleared.

docs.title: 4 · Score the evidence
docs.text:
Score Meaning 0 · Not yet No correct runnable result, or a critical shape/loss/gradient error remains 1 · With support Correct after documentation, a hint, or one material correction 2 · Independent Correct without help, with assertions and a clear explanation

Use the lower of theory and coding evidence for a domain.

If one item fails, follow its re-entry link, complete only that focused block, and retry the item. You never restart the whole course.
